headline: A thin day for core work: read Razin and co-authors' theory of on-policy distillation objectives (learning order across token positions, forward vs reverse KL landscapes) and the test-time symmetrization paper (O(log|G|) input rewritings provably recover what all rewritings give). The rest is extracurricular learning theory (information-theoretic benign overfitting, NeurIPS leverage-score and halfspace results) plus a few IR/RecSys systems papers. All 27 curator posts had already been listed on earlier days.

daily_picks.title: Local Feature Selection without Label or Feature Leakage for Interpretable Machine Learning Predictions
daily_picks.digest:
Setting and problem 
 In local (instance-wise) feature selection, a selector $\zeta$ outputs a mask $h\sim\zeta(x)$, $h\in\{0,1\}^d$. A predictor sees only $x\odot h$, where unselected entries are a distinct symbol $\emptyset$, so $h$ is recoverable from the input. The two are trained jointly:
$$\mathcal L(\zeta,f) = \frac1N\sum_i \mathbb E_{h_i\sim\zeta(x_i)}\big[L(f(x_i\odot h_i),y_i) + \lambda\|h_i\|\big].$$
The selected features are meant to be the explanation. Examples are L2X, INVASE, REAL-X and TabNet.


 The known failure (Jethani et al., 2103.01890 ) is that the selector can encode the prediction in which features it picks. One pixel per MNIST image then gives near-perfect accuracy. Table 1 gives a minimal example: $y = x_1 + x_2$ with independent binary features. The mask pattern alone recovers both unselected values, so the method gets 100% accuracy with 62.5% feature reduction.

Main idea 
 The paper formalizes two kinds of leakage, for every $(x,y,s^{\text{in}},s^{\text{ex}})$ in the support $\Omega$:


 
 Label leakage: $p(y\mid x[s^{\text{in}}]) \neq p(y\mid x[s^{\text{in}}], h[s^{\text{in}}]=1, h[s^{\text{ex}}]=0, \zeta)$. 
 Feature leakage: the same, with $x[s^{\text{ex}}]$ in place of $y$.

daily_picks.title: Reaching the End of Unbiasedness: Uncovering Implicit Limitations of Click-Based Learning to Rank
daily_picks.digest:
Setting and problem 
 Relevance is $R_{d\mid q} = P(R=1\mid d,q) \in [0,1]$, and ranking quality is $\mathcal R_q(y) = \sum_{d\in y}\lambda(\mathrm{rank}(d\mid y))\,R_{d\mid q}$. Clicks are biased. Under the affine model (Agarwal et al. 2019; Vardasbi et al. 2020),
$$P(C=1\mid d,k,q) = \alpha_k R_{d\mid q} + \beta_k,$$
which covers position bias ($\beta_k=0$) and trust bias. The standard affine estimator $\hat R_{d\mid q} = \frac1{|\mathcal D_q|}\sum_i (c_i(d) - \hat\beta_{k_i(d)})/\hat\alpha_{k_i(d)}$ is unbiased when $\hat\alpha,\hat\beta$ are correct.


 The field's usual recipe is: assume a click model, then derive an unbiased estimator for it. The paper runs this in reverse. It writes down the generic form of existing methods and asks which click behaviour they can possibly be unbiased for. These limitations follow from the form of the methods, not from their stated assumptions, which is why the paper calls them implicit.


 Definitions:


 
 Unbiasedness is per item: $\mathbb E[\hat R_{d\mid q}] = R_{d\mid q}$ for all $(d,q)$. 
 Consistency : $\lim_{|\mathcal D_q|\to\infty}\hat R_{d\mid q} = R_{d\mid q}$.

daily_picks.title: Posterior Network: Uncertainty Estimation without OOD Samples via Density-Based Pseudo-Counts
daily_picks.digest:
Setting and problem 
 Classification with $C$ classes. For each input $x^{(i)}$ the model should report two kinds of uncertainty. Aleatoric uncertainty is about the label $y^{(i)}$ given the categorical parameter $p^{(i)}$. Epistemic uncertainty is about $p^{(i)}$ itself. Ensembles and MC dropout represent the distribution $q^{(i)}$ over $p^{(i)}$ implicitly and need $S$ forward passes. The "Dirichlet" family (Prior Networks, Malinin & Gales 2018/2019) predicts $q^{(i)} = \mathrm{Dir}(\alpha^{(i)})$ in one pass, with mean $\bar p_c = \alpha_c/\alpha_0$, $\alpha_0 = \sum_c \alpha_c$.


 The paper lists four problems with Prior Networks:


 
 They need OOD samples at training time. 
 No finite OOD set can describe "everything else". 
 Nothing bounds $\int \alpha_0(x)\,dx$, so the network can give arbitrarily high confidence far from the data. 
 They can produce degenerate concentrations ($\alpha_c < 1$). 
 
 The goal is OOD-aware Dirichlet outputs trained only on in-distribution data, with no hand-set target concentrations.

Main idea 
 Take the conjugate update of a single categorical, $\mathrm{Dir}(\beta^{\text{prior}}) \to \mathrm{Dir}(\beta^{\text{prior}} + \beta^{\text{data}})$ with $\beta^{\text{data}}_c$ = class counts, and make the counts input-dependent. researchers.title: Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
researchers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our results show that ExecJudges agrees with NIST assessors at the level of the Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021. With a small number of human labels per topic, the ExecJudges-L variant agrees with NIST more than per-topic classifiers with the same labels on all seven collections, and either exceeds the agreement of LLM judges provided the same labels or is within about 0.05 of it in Krippendorff's alpha. The labels rank the official TREC DL runs with Kendall's tau of 0.87 to 0.94, and writing the programs incurs a one-time cost of $0.17 to $0.49 per topic, with no additional costs for grading. Our results suggest that ExecJudges offers a reproducible, inspectable, efficient and cost-effective alternative to LLM judges for labeling deep result pools for system evaluation or ranking improvements.
researchers.evidence: University of Waterloo, with Eugene Agichtein (Emory)
researchers.summary: Executable program judges replace per-document LLM relevance labels; NIST agreement on par with LLM judges on TREC DL.

papers.title: Which Tokens, in What Order, and How Fast? A Theoretical Analysis of On-Policy Distillation Objectives
papers.abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student language model to match a teacher model based on its own generations. When using OPD, one must choose whether to apply it at the sequence or token level and which divergence to minimize. However, despite the wide adoption of OPD in practice, the formal understanding of which OPD objective is appropriate for a given setting is limited. Toward addressing this gap, we theoretically analyze how the choice of OPD objective governs which tokens are prioritized, in what order, and how efficiently. Our analysis reveals that sequence-level OPD exhibits a future agreement bias, which myopic token-level objectives avoid. This bias induces a reverse learning order, in which sequence-level OPD first matches the teacher at later token positions, while at earlier positions it can favor tokens that are improbable under the teacher, and thus often undesirable. As for the choice of divergence, we prove that it strongly influences the amenability of OPD to gradient-based optimization. In particular, while the forward KL divergence enjoys a well-behaved objective landscape, other $f$-divergences, such as reverse KL, can suffer from vanishing gradients even when the student and teacher are far apart. Across language model post-training settings, we demonstrate the implications of these theoretical findings for which OPD objective is preferable, highlighting the importance of accounting for the interplay between the student, teacher, and task at hand.
papers.summary: Theory of on-policy distillation objectives. Sequence-level OPD has a 'future agreement bias' that makes it fit the teacher at later token positions first and can push early positions toward tokens the teacher finds improbable; token-level objectives avoid this. Forward KL gives a well-behaved landscape, while reverse KL and other f-divergences can have vanishing gradients even far from the teacher.
papers.why: A clean learning-order result for autoregressive objectives: which positions of a sequence get learned first and why, the same kind of question as how a GR model learns a docid tree level by level.

papers.title: Test-Time Symmetrization: Scaling Laws for Model-Agnostic Learning under Structure
papers.abstract: Test-time compute has emerged as a powerful way to improve the accuracy of language models at inference time, with scaling laws quantifying how accuracy improves with additional forward passes. Existing scaling laws, however, focus on repeated sampling from a fixed prompt, even though many tasks admit multiple equivalent representations of the same underlying problem. A graph does not depend on how its nodes are numbered, and a program does not depend on the names of its variables, yet language models can change their answers under such rewritings. In this paper, we study test-time symmetrization, which uses forward passes on rewritings of the input and aggregates the resulting answers over the group $G$ of rewritings. We prove that no amount of sampling and repeated decoding from a single representation can replace rewriting, while only $O(\log |G|)$ random rewritings suffice to recover the information provided by all $|G|$ rewritings. The same set of $O(\log |G|)$ rewritings provides simultaneous approximation across models, decoding rules, and sampled reasoning traces, and the logarithmic scaling is optimal in general. We validate the theory with experiments on Qwen2.5-7B, Phi-4-mini, Llama-3.1-8B, and Qwen2.5-14B, with chain-of-thought reasoning, on graph reasoning, logical deduction, and multiple-choice question answering. At the same number of forward passes, spending them on rewritings of the input is substantially more accurate than spending them on repeated sampling from the original prompt whenever the model's answer depends on how the input is written, and the number of rewritings needed grows only logarithmically with the number of possible rewritings, as the theory predicts. Our results provide a principled way to enforce symmetries at inference time when they cannot be built into the model, which we call model-agnostic symmetrization.
papers.summary: Test-time symmetrization: run the model on rewritings of the input (a group G of equivalent representations, e.g. node relabelings) and aggregate. Proves that repeated sampling from one representation cannot replace rewriting, that O(log|G|) random rewritings recover the information of all |G| (uniformly over models, decoders and traces), and that log scaling is optimal; confirmed on four 7-14B models.
papers.why: A test-time compute scaling law with a matching lower bound, stated about the LM's dependence on input representation rather than about sampling noise.

papers.title: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection
papers.abstract: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well, which neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds explain. We develop an information-theoretic framework that separates two things an interpolating learner does with its sample: storage, the information the trained model retains about its training labels, and expression, the information about the sample that reaches its predictions at fresh inputs. We first characterize the ideal model: for a loss l, the least complex l-sufficient representation is the Bayes act, whose entropy is the minimal sufficient complexity; this generalizes, and corrects, an earlier "lossless maximal compression" view of boosting. We then show that every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage, and bounds built on it (including CMI bounds), cannot tell interpolators apart. Expression can: excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V, the entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input, plus a modal-bias term, exactly so for binary labels. Benign overfitting is therefore vanishing expression, a picture that covers nearest-neighbour rules, averaging, minimum-norm least squares and double descent, and that links V to classical bias-variance decompositions and to model disagreement. Finally, V gives a model-selection criterion that needs no held-out labels. Among overparameterized learners on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost; at matched cost it also beats selection by conditional mutual information. We characterize when it fails and give remedies. Code: https://github.com/nnikolaou/GLMC
papers.summary: Splits what an interpolating learner does with its sample into storage (information about training labels kept in the model) and expression (information that reaches predictions at fresh inputs). Every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage-based (incl. CMI) bounds cannot separate interpolators; excess risk is bounded above and below by expressed information, and benign overfitting is vanishing expression. The quantity also gives a label-free model-selection rule.
papers.why: A sharp information-theoretic statement separating memorization from generalization, citable when positioning a memorization-based account of GR.

papers.title: Stability Does Not Mirror Plasticity: A Module-Level View of Declarative and Procedural Learning in Transformers
papers.abstract: Plasticity and stability in continual learning are typically studied at the entire-model level and in a task-agnostic manner, yet prior work has reported divergent conclusions across settings. Inspired by cognitive distinctions between declarative and procedural memory, we instead study how plasticity and stability vary across transformer modules and task types. In a controlled synthetic environment with clean measurement, we show a double dissociation: query-key (QK) and value-output (VO) projections are the most plastic on procedural tasks, whereas MLPs are the most plastic on declarative memorization. Stability, however, does not simply mirror plasticity: when learning a new procedure, updating QK retains over half of the stored declarative memory, while updating MLPs retains far less and updating VO loses roughly four-fifths. Targeted module reset-and-recovery experiments explain this asymmetry: plasticity tracks which module is best suited to a task's primary computation or storage, whereas stability depends on all ways the existing capability relies on that module, including access to information stored in other modules. Experiments on a realistic model and tasks broadly echo these asymmetric dynamics. Overall, our work shows that plasticity and stability depend on different aspects of a module's functional role, offering a task-dependent, module-level perspective on continual learning.
papers.summary: In a controlled synthetic setup, MLPs are the most plastic modules for declarative memorization and QK/VO projections for procedural tasks. Stability does not mirror this: learning a new procedure by updating QK keeps over half of the stored facts, updating MLPs keeps far less, updating VO loses about four fifths. Reset-and-recovery experiments explain the asymmetry by how other modules depend on each one.
papers.why: Clean phenomenon on where a transformer stores memorized facts vs procedures, with controlled measurements a theorist could model.

papers.title: General progress substitutes for specific training data in language models
papers.abstract: Language models acquire their capabilities from training data, and developers withhold data during training to keep models from learning capabilities that could be misused. How long this delays a capability, and how much data is needed to acquire it later, is unknown. Here we show that the general progress a model makes on the rest of its training data substitutes for the data that was withheld. We withheld the training signal for individual skills in models of chess, Othello, molecular strings, bracket languages and web text. The delay of a withheld skill in larger models was predicted from smaller ones. A chess model never explicitly trained to respond to check ranked the legal responses almost as well as a model that was. When models were then trained on the withheld data, they acquired the skill with a small fraction of the data needed from initialization, and this fraction decreased as the models progressed. A control rule of equal difficulty was learned much more slowly. A programming language withheld from the training text of a 7-billion-parameter model was regained in the same way. Data filtering therefore delays a capability, and the data required to regain it decreases as models improve.
papers.summary: Withholding the training signal for one skill (chess check responses, Othello, bracket languages, molecular strings, a programming language in a 7B model) only delays it: general progress on the rest of the data substitutes for the withheld data, the delay in large models is predictable from small ones, and the data needed to acquire the skill later shrinks as the model improves. A control rule of equal difficulty is learned much more slowly.
papers.why: Controlled phenomenon about transfer from general training to a specific skill, with scaling predictions, across several synthetic and natural domains.

papers.title: Differentiable Exact Learning
papers.abstract: We introduce a framework for differentiable exact learning that couples an unbounded external environment to a state-tracking neural controller, which we train on policy-trajectory observations (PTOs): expert behavior traces that expose observations and actions while hiding internal states. In addition to the learning framework, we introduce Differentiable Finite-State Transducers (DFSTs) which use multilinear updates, support log-parallel training, and emulate arbitrary finite-state controllers, yielding computational universality through environmental interaction. From tiny training datasets, compact DFSTs achieve extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal-simulation tasks. We replicate the success of DFSTs on RNNs and GRUs, thereby supporting a broader learning recipe: State-Tracking Controller + Unbounded External Environment + PTOs = Extreme Length Generalization. Beyond length generalization, our metric-extraction protocol recovers interpretable discrete controllers from trained DFSTs, which we prove equivalent to the target arithmetic and universal-simulation algorithms. Furthermore, for our Softmax DFST models, simply taking $\mathrm{argmax}$ over the transition probabilities yields discrete controllers which provably exactly perform universal Turing-machine simulation and binary arithmetic. Proving exact learning for the neural controllers requires assumptions, which we empirically support. We make our code, training recipes, model weights, and proof checkers publicly available at https://github.com/fanagor/DEL.
papers.summary: Couples a state-tracking neural controller (differentiable finite-state transducers, also RNNs/GRUs) with an unbounded external environment, trained on traces that expose observations and actions but hide states. Tiny datasets give extreme length generalization on arithmetic and universal simulation, and argmax over transitions provably yields controllers that exactly implement the target algorithms (under stated assumptions).
papers.why: Exact learning with a provable extracted algorithm, from Flammarion's group; a clean contrast to length-generalization failures of transformers.

papers.title: Two is better than one: optimizing binary rating scales for online platforms
papers.abstract: Online platforms often struggle with inflated, uninformative user ratings. This issue can be mitigated by better design of the data collection mechanism, for example through changing the phrasing of user questions. Previous work optimizes a single rating scale to best distinguish the inherent qualities of items under binary feedback. In this paper, we demonstrate the power of utilizing different rating scales for different users. First, we show that a designer can always split a single rating scale into two to improve item rankings. Next, we formally characterize the optimal design of multiple scales as a series of 0-1 step functions whose threshold values are evenly spaced. Finally, we consider an adaptive model where subsequent rating scales can depend on the responses from previous users and items are ranked by their full sequence of responses, and show that adaptivity leads to exponentially greater distinguishing power. All in all, our theoretical results show that using multiple rating scales significantly improves item rankings on platforms.
papers.summary: Designing binary rating questions to rank items under inflated feedback: splitting one rating scale into two always improves item ranking; the optimal set of scales is a series of 0-1 step functions with evenly spaced thresholds; adaptive scales chosen from earlier responses give exponentially greater distinguishing power.
papers.why: Small, exact results on how feedback design limits what a ranking can recover; a theory angle on recommender data collection.

papers.title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression
papers.abstract: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. Given a design matrix $A\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times d}$, a constraint set $C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^d$, and query access to $b\in\mathbb{R}^n$, we seek an approximate solution to $\min_{x\in C}\|Ax-b\|_2^2$ using as few queries as possible. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. Experiments on synthetic regression problems and a parametric heat conduction problem show lower regression error than standard baselines for similar query budget.
papers.summary: Active constrained least squares: ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores give query complexity O(d_eff(C) log d / eps^2), with d_eff(C) an anisotropic effective dimension of the constraint set, improved to 1/eps for convex constraints; matching lower bounds show d/eps^2 is unavoidable without convexity.
papers.why: Sharp sampling bounds driven by leverage scores, the same coherence quantity that decides when uniform coordinate sampling preserves geometry.

papers.title: Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation
papers.abstract: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.
papers.summary: Two-layer networks trained by SGD on a multi-index teacher in the proportional limit: first-layer weights orthogonal to the teacher subspace develop teacher-dependent spectral spikes in their Gram matrix, which inflate representation variance and hurt generalization. A tractable surrogate ('Decomposed Dynamics') has the same asymptotic test error as SGD; freezing the orthogonal part helps.
papers.why: Exact high-dimensional SGD dynamics showing how feature learning outside the signal subspace harms generalization.

papers.title: Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
papers.abstract: Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution $p$ using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to $p$) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path. In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when $p$ satisfies a Poincar\'e inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution $p$, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of $p$. We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify $p$? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincar\'e constant of $p$, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.
papers.summary: Avoiding path-space analysis, the error of a diffusion sampler with an imperfect score need not accumulate polynomially with the horizon when the target satisfies a Poincare inequality; more generally the error is controlled in a weaker metric for any target. Given a score-error bound and a Poincare constant, the sampler is nearly information-theoretically optimal in TV.
papers.why: Sharp sampling-error theory for diffusion (Moitra, Risteski); background for diffusion-LM theory.

papers.title: Rare-Tail Statistics For Learning Biased Gaussian Halfspaces with Label Noise
papers.abstract: We revisit the classical problem of learning general Gaussian halfspaces in the presence of label noise, with particular focus on the large-bias regime, where information-computation gaps are conjectured in several standard label-noise models. Concretely, we present and analyze the rare-tail mean estimator, an extremely simple one-shot statistic that averages only the observed minority class. In the large-bias regime, classical Averaging (Servedio, 1999) and related global first-moment statistics are provably suboptimal, while the rare-tail mean estimator recovers the target halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate (modulo log factors) under a broad class of label noise models, including probit noise and margin-dependent noise with very slow decay away from the boundary. Notably, our guarantees allow labels arbitrarily close to the decision boundary to be nearly random, while still giving strong directional recovery from a small number of samples. The estimator also cleanly interpolates between the noiseless and noisy regimes: without noise, it attains the same sample rate as classical separability-based methods for realizable halfspaces, and under low noise, or noise that decays away from the boundary, it keeps this rate even after linear separability has been destroyed. As an application, we consider a two-stage curriculum in which source samples, whose noise may be arbitrarily close to $1/2$ near the boundary and decay very slowly away from it, precede target samples, whose noise flips every label at the same rate, i.e., random classification noise (RCN). Since both stages share the same Bayes optimal halfspace, our estimator supplies the directional warm start needed by existing refinement routines, and together they learn the RCN target at the information-theoretic sample rate in the large-bias regime, up to log factors.
papers.summary: Learning biased Gaussian halfspaces under label noise: averaging only the minority class (rare-tail mean) recovers the direction at the information-theoretic sample rate in the large-bias regime, where global first-moment methods are provably suboptimal, under probit and slowly decaying margin noise.
papers.why: A one-line estimator with matching rates; clean learning theory for the long-tail regime.

papers.title: Monoculture Robust Learning
papers.abstract: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is $\rho$-replicable, then running it independently $k$ times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with $k$, controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and $\rho$. We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to $\gamma$ can require a sample-size multiplier of $t = \Omega(\log(1/\gamma))$.
papers.summary: Monoculture robustness in PAC learning: from one dataset, output k accurate hypotheses whose joint failure is comparable to training on k independent datasets. If the base learner is rho-replicable, k independent runs on the same sample drive the individual conjunctive error down exponentially in k; a lower bound shows a sample-size multiplier Omega(log 1/gamma) can be necessary.
papers.why: New clean notion with a surprising link to replicability (Kleinberg, Reingold).

papers.title: Nearly Tight Almost Sure Convergence Rates for the Last iterate of SGD
papers.abstract: We study the almost sure convergence of the last-iterate optimization error of Stochastic (sub)Gradient Descent (SGD) for convex objectives. For smooth objectives, we establish convergence rates of order $k^{-1/3}$ when a stationary minimizer exists, and $k^{-1/4}$ otherwise, up to polylogarithmic factors, where $k$ denotes the iteration counter. We further show that the latter rate extends to nonsmooth convex objectives. All these rates are achieved by deterministic, anytime stepsize policies. Finally, we establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponents $-1/3$ and $-1/4$ are optimal, up to polylogarithmic factors, for the corresponding problem classes.
papers.summary: Almost-sure last-iterate rates for SGD on convex objectives: k^{-1/3} for smooth objectives with a stationary minimizer, k^{-1/4} otherwise and for nonsmooth objectives, with anytime step sizes, and matching lower bounds up to logs.
papers.why: Tight rates with lower bounds for the last iterate of SGD.

papers.title: The Spectral Distribution of Matrix Least Squares Solutions, and the Ellipsoid Fitting Problem
papers.abstract: We study the spectral distribution of the least squares solution to a random linear system whose unknown is a symmetric matrix. In the normalized and isotropic setting, we derive a closed-form description of the support of the spectral distribution. As an application, we consider the ellipsoid fitting problem: given $n$ standard Gaussian vectors in $\mathbb{R}^d$, does there exist a centered ellipsoid passing through all of them? It was recently shown that this problem has a sharp phase transition at $n \approx d^2/4$. On the satisfiability side, unlike earlier results, these sharp results do not rely on least squares candidates. We show that the least squares candidates considered in earlier works have a threshold of positive semi-definiteness at $n \approx d^2/10$, which was previously observed numerically and predicted non-rigorously using statistical physics methods. Moreover, we show that the corresponding least squares dual certificates have a threshold of positive definiteness at $n \approx 2d^2/5$. Our approach combines several matrix concentration tools. A key technical ingredient, which may be of independent interest, is showing that a certain kernel matrix is well-conditioned with high probability until $n \approx d^2/2$.
papers.summary: Closed-form support of the spectral distribution of the least-squares solution to a random linear system in a symmetric matrix. Application to ellipsoid fitting through n Gaussian points in R^d: the least-squares candidate is PSD only up to n ~ d^2/10 (proving a statistical-physics prediction) and its dual certificate up to n ~ 2d^2/5, below the true threshold d^2/4.

papers.title: Copying along Arithmetic Progressions Cannot Simulate Interleaving with Polylogarithmic Loss
papers.abstract: Two classical ways to compress a word are straight-line programs (SLPs), which build it by concatenating smaller pieces, and the Lempel-Ziv 77 (LZ77) factorisation, which copies earlier parts of it; their sizes are measures of repetitiveness. LZ77 approximates the smallest SLP efficiently: it has no more factors than a smallest SLP has size, and yields an SLP at most a logarithmic factor larger in near-linear time. Motivated by online prediction, Kosoy introduced zipline programs, which are analogous to SLPs but interleave their pieces round-robin instead of concatenating them. Her generalisation of LZ77, the arithmetic repetition system, describes a word by copies from one arithmetic progression of positions to a later one. Do arithmetic repetition systems approximate the smallest zipline program as well? Kosoy proved that the least size $\mathrm{ARC}(x)$ of an arithmetic repetition system for a word $x$ of length $n$ is at most a factor $O(n^{1/3})$ larger than the least size $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ of a zipline program for it, and asked whether this factor is tight. Her polynomial-time next-letter predictor makes $O(\mathrm{ARC}(x)\log n)$ mistakes, so a polylogarithmic factor would bound its mistakes by $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$, which no known polynomial-time predictor achieves. We show that the optimal exponent is $1/4$, not $1/3$: $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \le 2n^{1/4}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ for every word $x$, and at every large enough length $n$ some binary word has $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \ge n^{1/4-o(1)}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$.
papers.summary: Answers Kosoy's question on compressing words by interleaving: arithmetic repetition systems are within a factor 2n^{1/4} of the smallest zipline program, and some binary words need n^{1/4-o(1)}, so the optimal exponent is 1/4, not 1/3. This rules out a polylog mistake bound for Kosoy's polynomial-time next-letter predictor via this route.
papers.why: Tight result linking compression to online next-token prediction mistake bounds.

papers.title: Can Programs Replace LLM Judges? Executable Program Judges for Scalable and Efficient Relevance Labeling
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) judges have become a common way to create large-scale relevance judgments for retrieval evaluation. However, each judgment requires a potentially expensive call to a frontier model, and the judgments are hard to interpret and may not be reproducible. In this paper, we ask whether an LLM can write a readable program for each topic that replaces its per-document judgments. To address these issues, we propose ExecJudges, a method for generating fast, inspectable and scalable judges for automatic relevance labeling. Specifically, ExecJudges uses a frontier LLM to turn assessment guidelines into executable programs, which rely only on lexical matching, standard NLP libraries like parsers, and pool statistics. An ExecJudges-L variant also uses examples of human labels if available. We evaluate ExecJudges on seven TREC collections by comparing the produced labels with trained NIST assessors, frontier LLM judges, and recently proposed per-topic classifiers. Our results show that ExecJudges agrees with NIST assessors at the level of the Claude Sonnet 5.5 LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021. With a small number of human labels per topic, the ExecJudges-L variant agrees with NIST more than per-topic classifiers with the same labels on all seven collections, and either exceeds the agreement of LLM judges provided the same labels or is within about 0.05 of it in Krippendorff's alpha. The labels rank the official TREC DL runs with Kendall's tau of 0.87 to 0.94, and writing the programs incurs a one-time cost of $0.17 to $0.49 per topic, with no additional costs for grading. Our results suggest that ExecJudges offers a reproducible, inspectable, efficient and cost-effective alternative to LLM judges for labeling deep result pools for system evaluation or ranking improvements.
papers.summary: ExecJudges: a frontier LLM writes, per TREC topic, an executable lexical program that labels relevance. Agreement with NIST assessors matches LLM judges on TREC DL 2019-2021, ranks official runs with Kendall's tau 0.87-0.94, at $0.17-0.49 per topic once.

papers.title: Optimize the Cob, Then the Kernel: Optimizing Beam Search for Generative Recommendation Inference
papers.abstract: Generative recommendation (GR) inference differs substantially from conventional LLM serving, featuring long input sequences, wide beam search, and only a few fixed output tokens. Existing LLM serving engines such as vLLM process beams as batched independent sequences, causing redundant KV cache accesses over the shared prompt prefix. Furthermore, vLLM executes each beam search generation step as a separate engine invocation, incurring host-side beam processing overhead between decoding steps and substantial runtime KV block management in PagedAttention. Using Tree Attention, we concatenate beams along the sequence dimension to eliminate redundant KV accesses, and further optimize execution through pre-generated partial-attention masks, static KV cache allocation, loop-unrolled generation dispatch, TorchAir graph compilation, automatic operator fusion, and vocabulary-constrained decoding. Without the use of custom kernels, our approach reduces end-to-end latency by up to 25x over vLLM on Ascend NPUs, and achieves generation latency comparable to a SOTA solution using custom kernels, showing that the generation pipeline should be optimized holistically before resorting to custom kernel development.
papers.summary: Serving generative recommenders: tree attention over beams to avoid repeated KV reads of the shared prefix, static KV allocation, unrolled generation and constrained decoding give up to 25x lower latency than vLLM on Ascend NPUs without custom kernels.

papers.title: CONCORD-Rec: Catalog-Conditioned Modality Utility for Semantic-ID Diffusion Recommendation
papers.abstract: Multimodal generative recommendation with discrete semantic identifiers (SIDs) requires distinguishing historical modalities that merely alter token predictions from those that genuinely reduce catalog-level ambiguity. When audiovisual, visual, or textual streams are missing, degraded, or semantically conflicting, uniform fusion and unconstrained token gates can propagate misleading content across iterative denoising steps. We propose CONCORD-Rec, a reliability-conditioned discrete diffusion recommender supervised by counterfactual catalog-partition utility. Given a fixed tokenizer and a partially masked SID state, CONCORD-Rec evaluates out-of-fold teacher coalitions over the exact feasible catalog support and aggregates item posteriors across the target code partition at each unresolved position. Rather than distilling raw token probabilities directly, the resulting counterfactual loss differences supervise an availability-masked tokenwise gate that allocates bounded modality residuals around a behavioral denoiser while retaining an exact behavioral fallback slot. We establish theoretical fixed-support ranking stability bounds under gate perturbations and evaluate position-level and code-conditional allocation across audiovisual and image-text recommendation benchmarks under controlled missingness, signal degradation, and semantic conflict. Across 20 source-compatible protocol-dataset rows, CONCORD-Rec improves NDCG by 4%; under matched 30% conflict it improves NDCG by 14.63%. The full-vs-uniform-T=16 sweep improves quality by 2.00-3.58% while reducing p95 latency by up to 86.89%.
papers.summary: Discrete-diffusion recommender over semantic IDs with a reliability gate on modalities, trained from counterfactual catalog-partition utility; robust to missing or conflicting modalities (+4% NDCG overall, +14.6% under 30% conflict).

papers.title: VIBRA: Backward-Compatible Cross-Modal Retrieval with Consensus Barycenters
papers.abstract: Backward-compatible retrieval enables a new encoder to query the gallery that an old model has already encoded, so that a cross-modal retrieval system can be upgraded without re-encoding billions of items. Existing compatible methods either fit the old query and stay near the accuracy of the old model, or run the old and the new encoder for every query. We propose VIBRA, which matches relevance on the old gallery, corrects the errors of a single model with the barycenter of several views, which is itself a query in the old space, and trains the new encoder to inherit this consensus, so that models absent at deployment still shape every query. We show that the barycenter gains margin over the average of its views exactly when their hardest irrelevant items differ, and we characterize the share of this gain that one encoder can reach. On five benchmarks with five upgrades among six CLIP, MetaCLIP and SigLIP2 backbones, VIBRA is the best compatible method in all 50 settings, improving Recall@1 by up to 5.6 points over the strongest baseline and by up to 18.0 points over the old model, while adding less than 1 ms to the latency of the new encoder.
papers.summary: Backward-compatible cross-modal retrieval: train the new encoder to match a barycenter of several old-space views, with a margin argument for when the barycenter helps; best compatible method in 50 upgrade settings among CLIP/SigLIP2 backbones.

papers.title: X-split Argus: Learning Reusable History Tokens for Efficient CTR Prediction
papers.comments: Alexander Ploshkin, Nikita Stepanov and Alexey Pismenny contributed equally to this work
papers.abstract: Accurate click-through rate (CTR) prediction depends on user representations that capture both persistent preferences and recent intent, yet processing extensive behavioral histories for every ranking request is costly under production compute and latency constraints. We present X-split ARGUS, a framework for ad ranking whose history compressor and online ranker are trained end to end. The compressor encodes past interactions into a compact set of tokens that are computed offline and reused across candidates, while the online ranker scores ads through cross-attention to these tokens and representations of recent events. Training combines an autoregressive loss for click feedback with distillation of candidate-specific click logits from a larger teacher that scores each candidate using the uncompressed history. The number of compressed history tokens and the length of recent history can be adjusted to fit serving compute and latency budgets. Offline evaluation shows a 0.81% relative reduction in normalized entropy (NE) compared with the production baseline. Deployment in a large-scale real-time bidding system increases online inference cost by 15% relative to the production baseline. An online A/B test against this baseline yields relative gains of 4.65% in a business metric reflecting the monetary value of conversions generated for advertisers and 2.96% in clicks.
papers.summary: Ad ranking that compresses long user histories offline into reusable tokens and scores candidates by cross-attention, trained end to end with distillation from an uncompressed teacher; online gains in a production bidding system.

papers.title: LusoClin: A Synthetic Clinical Note Dataset for Medical Information Retrieval in European Portuguese
papers.abstract: Access to large-scale clinical text collections is crucial for advancing medical information retrieval research, including clinical note search, patient cohort identification, and domain-adapted retrieval models. However, real clinical notes are rarely available due to privacy regulations, which particularly limits progress for low-resource languages such as European Portuguese. We present LusoClin, a publicly released dataset of synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, created to support privacy-preserving research on clinical text retrieval. LusoClin was generated by pre-processing real clinical data, fine-tuning the open-source Llama 3.2 (3B) instruction-tuned model using Quantized Low-Rank Adaptation, and applying prompt-based clinical note generation. To facilitate semantic indexing and clinical search, the notes are automatically annotated with clinical entities using a BERT-based model. We evaluate LusoClin in terms of utility, fidelity, diversity, and privacy using automatic metrics and human evaluation. Results indicate that the dataset captures clinically relevant language patterns and can support downstream IR applications such as clinical document retrieval and domain-specific model adaptation, although annotators can often distinguish synthetic from real notes and some medical inconsistencies persist.
papers.summary: Synthetic clinical notes in European Portuguese, generated by a fine-tuned Llama 3.2 3B and annotated with entities, released for medical IR research; evaluated for utility, fidelity, diversity and privacy.

papers.title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
papers.comments: Ongoing work. 67 pages with 34 figures and 37 tables. Project website: https://hackerchenzhuo.github.io/knowme-research-ai/en/ GitHub: https://github.com/hackerchenzhuo/knowme-research-ai
papers.abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.
papers.summary: KnowMe Paper Radar: a paper-recommendation tool combining topical relevance, recency, author histories and collaboration paths with inspectable score components; cached abstracts raise NDCG@10 from 0.41 to 0.60 on expert-judged tasks.
